questions.q: Per this lesson, why is standardization described as 'free complexity reduction' rather than just a stylistic preference?
options: Because Salesforce charges extra for maintaining more than one page layout
Because standardized processes never require any maintenance at all
Because there's genuinely only one version of a layout, process, or rule set to test, document, train on, and fix, which measurably reduces the amount of system there is to reason about
Because standardized processes automatically adapt to any team's needs without configuration
questions.explain: The lesson argues standardization is a real, measurable reduction in how much system exists to maintain -- one layout, one approval process, one set of automation rules, as opposed to a different version per team.

questions.q: What real cost does this lesson identify when a single global approval threshold is applied to teams with very different deal sizes?
options: No real cost exists -- a single threshold always works equally well for every team
The cost only affects the IT department, never the sales teams themselves
Salesforce technically prevents approval processes from having more than one threshold

The threshold is either too low for a team closing large deals (causing approval fatigue on low-risk deals) or too high for a team closing small, frequent deals (letting genuinely risky deals through without proper review)
questions.explain: Forcing every team into the same threshold isn't neutral -- it's a real cost paid by whichever teams' actual deal sizes don't match the single number chosen.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the strongest configuration-based tool for handling genuine differences between teams without forking the whole system into separate, parallel processes?
options: Record Types, combined with dynamic page layouts and approval process entry criteria scoped by Record Type or business unit
Building a completely separate Salesforce org for each team
Disabling standardization entirely and letting each team build its own spreadsheet-based process
Granting every team 'Modify All' permission so they can customize freely
questions.explain: Record Types and criteria scoped by Record Type let a single underlying system present different, team-appropriate experiences while keeping one system to maintain -- getting most of standardization's benefit while still letting genuinely different parts actually differ.

questions.q: What is a 'shadow process,' as described in this lesson, and why does it matter to this tradeoff?
options: A second, officially sanctioned Salesforce automation that runs in parallel with the main one

An informal workaround, like spreadsheets or out-of-system approvals, that a team builds when the standard process doesn't fit their actual work -- a real, often invisible cost of forcing an ill-fitting standard
A Salesforce feature that automatically hides fields a user doesn't need
The backup copy of an approval process kept in a sandbox
questions.explain: A shadow process is the real-world consequence of forcing a team into a standard that doesn't fit -- it doesn't show up as a support ticket, so it's easy for whoever decided the standard to miss it entirely while it quietly damages data quality and adoption.

questions.q: How does this lesson reframe the standardization-vs-flexibility decision, rather than treating it as all-or-nothing?
options: As a single binary choice: either standardize everything or standardize nothing
As a decision that should always default to maximum flexibility regardless of maintenance cost
As a question of standardizing what's genuinely common across every team, while identifying what looks common but is actually different once the owning team is asked
As a decision that only applies to Apex code, never to declarative processes
questions.explain: The lesson's core reframe is to split a process into pieces -- some genuinely universal, some only superficially similar -- rather than deciding standardization as one all-or-nothing choice for the whole process.
